entry.title: What’s Under the Hood of an AI Agent

link.title: What’s Under the Hood of an AI Agent

entry.content:
← Back to home

A plain-language guide · no jargon required

What's really
happening under the hood of an AI agent

It feels like magic. It isn't. It's a very well-read brain, wired into a workshop.

Written for someone who has never touched code — so that the next time an "AI agent" does something impressive, you can picture exactly how it pulled it off.

Start here

Two parts, always

Every AI agent — the coding assistant, the research assistant, the little bot that books your meetings — is built from just two things stacked together.

There's the model, which is the brain: it thinks, reads, and writes. And there's the harness, which is the workshop built around that brain: it gives the brain memory, tools, instructions, and a way to actually do things in the world.

Keep these two straight and the rest of this page falls into place. Almost everything that looks magical is really just the harness handing the brain the right thing at the right moment.

◆ The model — the brain

Knows & reasons

  • Read an enormous amount once, long ago
  • Can reason, explain, translate, write
  • Great at language and patterns
  • On its own: no memory, no internet, no hands
▲ The harness — the workshop

Remembers & acts

  • Keeps notes so nothing is forgotten
  • Hands the brain tools (search, calculator, calendar)
  • Pins up instructions for the job
  • Runs the loop that turns thinking into doing

The model

A brilliant person in a sealed room

Picture the smartest, most well-read person you know. Now lock them in a room with no phone, no internet, and no way to remember today once it's over. Slide a question under the door on a piece of paper, and they slide back a beautifully written answer. That is a model.

It has read a staggering amount — books, articles, conversations, code — but all of that reading stopped at some point in the past. So the model is extraordinary at thinking, explaining, and writing, and helpless at anything that needs fresh information or action.

Can do

Reason with what it knows

Explain a tax rule, draft an email, spot a bug in code, summarise a messy paragraph, translate a menu.

Can't do — alone

Reach the live world

Tell you today's weather, open your files, send a message, or remember what you said yesterday.

This is the crucial idea: the model by itself can only talk. Everything else — looking things up, remembering, taking action — is the harness's job. Which is exactly where we go next.

One more thing people mix up: the model's capabilities are just how good the brain is — how well it reasons, how carefully it follows instructions, how much it can hold in its head at once. A stronger model is a smarter person in the room. It still can't see outside the room. That's a harness problem, not a brain problem.

The harness

The workshop around the brain

The harness is the room set up around that sealed-off genius. On its own the brain can only answer notes. The harness is what turns it into a worker who gets things done. It does four jobs.

1 · It keeps memory

The brain forgets everything between notes. The harness keeps a running transcript so the conversation actually builds on itself.

2 · It hands over tools

A phone to the weather service, a calculator, a way to read a file. The brain asks; the harness fetches.

3 · It pins up the instructions

A standing note above the desk saying who this worker is and how to behave. (That's the system prompt — coming up.)

4 · It runs the loop

Think, act, look at the result, think again — over and over, until the job is done. This loop is the whole trick.

A model is a brain. An agent is a brain the harness has given hands, memory, and a to-do list.

The loop

How thinking becomes doing

Here's the rhythm every agent runs on. It's not a single flash of genius — it's a patient loop, repeated as many times as the task needs.

The agent loop

01 · Think
Plan
The brain decides what it needs next.
→
02 · Act
Use a tool
It asks the harness to fetch or do something.
→
03 · Observe
Read result
The harness hands back what happened.
↺
04 · Repeat
or Answer
Loop again, or reply when done.

Now let's watch it run on the simplest possible question.

Toy example #1

"What's the temperature in Mumbai today?"

You'd think the AI just knows this. It doesn't — remember, the brain has been sealed in the room since before today existed. Step through what actually happens. Click along.

The model · the brain
The harness · the workshop
Note passed

Notice what happened: the brain never knew the temperature. It knew it needed the temperature, knew which tool to reach for, and knew how to phrase the answer once the harness handed back the number. The intelligence is in the reasoning; the fresh fact came from a tool. That division of labour is the entire game.

Tools

What a "tool" actually is

A tool is just a specific action the harness knows how to perform on the brain's behalf. The weather lookup was one. But the same idea covers everything an agent can do rather than just say:

Search the web
Fetch a live page or search result.
Read a file
Open a document on your computer.
Run a calculation
Do maths reliably, not by "feel".
Send a message
Post to Slack, email a colleague.
Edit code
Change a line in a real file and save it.
Check a calendar
See when you're free, book a slot.

The brain never touches any of these directly. It writes a little request — "read the file report.txt" — and the harness carries it out and reports back. Give an agent more tools and it can do more; take them away and even a genius model can only chat. An agent's real-world power is mostly a question of which tools it's been handed.

The system prompt

The job description pinned above the desk

Here's a puzzle. A sales agent and a marketing agent might run on the exact same brain — the same model. So why do they behave so differently?

Because of the note pinned above each one's desk. That standing instruction is called the system prompt: it tells the brain who it is, what it's here to do, what tone to use, and what to avoid — before a single question arrives. Same brilliant employee; two completely different job descriptions.

System prompt · Sales

"You are a sales assistant."

Qualify the lead, understand their budget, move toward booking a demo. Be warm, persuasive, and concrete about pricing. Never over-promise.

System prompt · Marketing

"You are a marketing strategist."

Find the audience, sharpen the message, draft campaign copy. Think in themes and channels. Favour clarity and brand voice over closing a single deal.

Swap those two notes and the sales agent starts writing campaigns while the marketing agent starts chasing deals — with no change to the underlying model at all. The system prompt is how one brain becomes a hundred different specialists. It's also where a company bakes in its rules: "always cite your source", "never share internal pricing", "reply in Hindi if the customer writes in Hindi".

Skills

Recipe cards in the drawer

A system prompt sets the overall job. But some tasks have a right way of being done that's too detailed to keep pinned on the wall all the time. That's what a skill is: a written playbook the worker pulls out of a drawer only when a matching task comes up.

Think of a folder of recipe cards. Each card has a title, a note about when to use it, and step-by-step instructions. The worker glances at the titles, and when a task matches — "ah, the customer wants a PowerPoint" — it pulls that one card and follows it.

A drawer of skills

Make a slide deck
When someone asks for a presentation → build clean slides, one idea each.
Write in our brand voice
When drafting anything public → use the tone guide, avoid these words.
Do expense reports
When handed receipts → sort, total, flag anything over the limit.

So how do people write a skill?

This is the reassuring part: a skill is mostly just clear instructions written in plain English — not code. You write down, as if training a new hire, three things: a short name, a line about when to use it, and the steps to follow. You can also tuck in an example or a checklist. The harness keeps this in the drawer and slips it to the brain at the right moment.

That's why skills are so powerful for ordinary teams: your best salesperson can capture how they actually do it in a page of instructions, and every agent can now follow that recipe perfectly, every time. Tools give an agent new hands; skills give it new know-how.

Toy example #2 · scaling up

Now the hard task: "Research this market for me"

A quick weather lookup is one trip around the loop. But suppose you ask for something big — "Put together market research on electric scooters in India: the main players, their pricing, what customers complain about, and where the gaps are."

One worker could grind through this alone, tool call after tool call. But it's slow, and it's a lot to hold in one head. So a capable harness does what a good manager does: it breaks the job into pieces and hands each piece to its own copy of the worker, all at once.

One manager, several agents working in parallel

Lead agent — splits the job & combines the findings
Agent A
List the main brands & models
Agent B
Gather pricing across sellers
Agent C
Read reviews for complaints
Agent D
Spot gaps & opportunities

Each sub-agent runs its own think–act–observe loop, using search and file tools, following any relevant skills. When they finish, they hand their findings back to the lead agent, which reads all four, resolves overlaps, and writes the single report you asked for.

That's the whole shape of "complex AI work". Not one impossibly-clever step — but a lot of simple loops, run in parallel, then stitched together. The same pattern builds a piece of software, plans an event, or reconciles a spreadsheet.

The concrete example

Where you've seen all of this: a coding agent

A coding assistant like Claude Code is exactly the machine we've described, aimed at one profession. The brain is the same kind of model. Its tools are things a programmer needs: read a file, edit a file, run the program, search the project. Its system prompt says "you are a careful software engineer." Its skills are playbooks like "how to write a good commit" or "how we structure tests here." And it runs the same loop — read the code, make a change, run it, see the error, fix it, repeat — until the feature works.

Now here's the leap: nothing about that shape is specific to coding. Swap the tools and the instructions and you have a coworker for a different job entirely.

Coding agent

Tools: edit files, run code, search a codebase.
Prompt: "careful engineer."
Skills: testing, commit style.

Office coworker agent

Tools: read documents, send email, build a deck, check the calendar.
Prompt: "helpful operations assistant."
Skills: your report format, your brand voice.

Same brain. Same harness idea. Same loop. Just a different kit on the desk. That's why one underlying technology can show up as a coding helper, a research analyst, a sales rep, and a marketing strategist — the differences you notice are almost entirely tools, system prompt, and skills, not four different kinds of intelligence.

The whole thing, in one breath

So, no magic

  1. A model is a brilliant, well-read brain that can only think, read, and write — sealed off from today's world.
  2. A harness is the workshop around it: memory, tools, instructions, and a loop.
  3. Tools are the specific actions the harness performs for the brain — a weather lookup, a file edit, a message. They're how an agent does instead of just talks.
  4. The system prompt is the job description that turns one brain into a sales rep, a marketer, or an engineer.
  5. Skills are plain-English recipe cards the worker pulls out when a matching task appears — new know-how, no code required.
  6. Hard jobs are just many small loops run in parallel by several sub-agents and stitched together by a lead.

Next time an agent does something that makes you go "how did it know that?" — you can answer your own question. It didn't know. It figured out what it needed, reached for the right tool, read the result, and told you. Patiently, in a loop. That's the machine.

← Back to home

A plain-language explainer · model + harness + tools + skills

Made to be read at your own pace. Come back to it whenever the jargon piles up.
entry.summary: A plain-language, no-jargon explainer of how AI agents actually work — the model (the brain), the harness (the workshop), tools, system prompts, skills, and the think-act-observe loop.

entry.title: LLM Inference — A Learning Path
entry.content:
← Back to home
Curated reading path · LLM inference

Learning LLMinference, in order.

Five stages, foundations first. Work down the chain instead of jumping to the fast tricks.

Stages5
Resources14
OrderSequential

Adapted from a LinkedIn post on learning LLM inference. Eleven of the fourteen links are posts from Paolo Perrone’s Hardware & Inference series on The AI Engineer; the other three are standalone resources by Brendan Bycroft, Horace He, and Aleksa Gordić.

Signal chain
  1. 1 Foundations
  2. 2 Transformers
  3. 3 GPU & hardware
  4. 4 Optimization
  5. 5 Engines
01

Foundations of LLM inference

Every LLM call follows this path. Get the vocabulary and the request lifecycle down before anything else.

Tokenization Forward pass Autoregressive generation Prefill & decode KV cache TTFT & ITL Throughput vs latency
01·Atheaiengineer.substack.com

What is Inference?

Paolo Perrone. Why reading is fast and writing is slow: inference splits into a parallel prefill (the whole prompt in one pass) and a serial decode (one token at a time), and nearly every cost, latency, and KV-cache question traces back to that difference.
01·Btheaiengineer.substack.com

Why is Inference Slow and Expensive?

Paolo Perrone. The economics: decode is bound by memory bandwidth, not compute (the “memory wall”), which is why output tokens cost several times more than input, why a faster GPU alone doesn’t help, and why the KV cache makes long conversations more expensive.
02

Basic transformer concepts

You don’t need to become a transformer researcher — but you should understand the computations inference engines are optimizing.

Transformer block Embeddings Self-attention QKV vectors
02·Abbycroft.net/llm

LLM Visualization

Brendan Bycroft. An interactive 3D walkthrough of a GPT-style model running a single-token inference. Rotate and zoom through embeddings, self-attention, the QKV projections, and the feed-forward layers, right down to individual multiply-adds. Best on desktop.
03

GPU & hardware fundamentals

Most inference bottlenecks are hardware bottlenecks. Understanding the GPU changes how you reason about performance.

GPU architecture Streaming Multiprocessors HBM vs SRAM Memory bandwidth FLOPS Compute-bound vs memory-bound
03·Atheaiengineer.substack.com

What is a GPU?

Paolo Perrone. The chip’s internals for AI: streaming multiprocessors, CUDA cores, tensor cores, and HBM — and why memory bandwidth and VRAM capacity matter more than raw TFLOPS for most inference workloads.
03·Btheaiengineer.substack.com

Why Does AI Need a GPU?

Paolo Perrone. The architectural argument: a neural net is billions of independent multiply-adds, the embarrassingly parallel work thousands of simple GPU cores do at once and a few big CPU cores cannot — plus the cases where a CPU is still the right call.
03·Ctheaiengineer.substack.com

H100 vs H200 vs B200

Paolo Perrone. A buyer’s framework across NVIDIA’s three current datacenter GPUs, decided in priority order by memory capacity, bandwidth, compute, and NVLink: H100 for $/token, H200 for bandwidth-bound decode, B200 for FP4 and rack scale.
03·Dtheaiengineer.substack.com

Why Your Multi-GPU Training Job Keeps Dying

Paolo Perrone. The four ways a small multi-GPU run kills itself — NCCL sync timeouts, one straggler GPU, uneven per-rank memory, un-resumable checkpoints — and the per-rank logging that names which one before you need it. (Training-side, but the same GPU/collective mechanics.)
03·Ehorace.io/brrr_intro.html

Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles

Horace He (2022). Decomposes deep-learning runtime into three regimes — compute, memory bandwidth, and overhead — and shows how to tell which one is throttling you, and therefore which optimizations will actually help. The canonical grounding for “compute-bound vs memory-bound.”
04

Inference optimization techniques

How modern inference systems actually get fast — the techniques the engines in stage 5 are built around.

Quantization PagedAttention FlashAttention Chunked prefill Speculative decoding Prompt caching Continuous batching
04·Atheaiengineer.substack.com

What is Quantization?

Paolo Perrone. Lossy compression for model weights — the “JPEG trick” that drops a 70B model from ~140 GB to ~35 GB. Covers the FP16→INT4/NF4 mechanics, PTQ vs QAT, why 4-bit keeps ~99% of quality, and where it degrades (small models, math and reasoning).
04·Btheaiengineer.substack.com

Quantization in Practice: GPTQ vs AWQ vs GGUF

Paolo Perrone. The practical format pick, with the punchline that the kernel (Marlin) matters more than the format: AWQ for vLLM on NVIDIA, GGUF Q4_K_M for CPU/Apple, GPTQ if you’re already shipping it. Same weights can run 10x apart on the right vs wrong kernel.
05

Inference engines

Different engines for different workloads. Match the tool to the shape of the traffic.

vLLM — high-throughput SGLang — shared context llama.cpp — CPU / edge TensorRT-LLM — max NVIDIA
05·Atheaiengineer.substack.com

vLLM vs Ollama vs SGLang vs TensorRT-LLM

Paolo Perrone. Head-to-head on the four serving engines: Ollama for local dev, vLLM as the production default (PagedAttention), SGLang when requests share context (RadixAttention), TensorRT-LLM for max NVIDIA throughput — with a decision tree and the note that TGI is now maintenance-mode.
05·Btheaiengineer.substack.com

Should You Self-Host Inference?

Paolo Perrone. The economics of hosted API vs managed deployment vs full self-hosting, decided in veto order (sovereignty, people, volume, model access). Breakeven sits near ~2M tokens/day, the MLOps salary dwarfs the GPU, and most teams land on a hybrid.
05·Ctheaiengineer.substack.com

What Breaks When You Self-Host an LLM

Paolo Perrone. The four undocumented handoffs that break a self-hosted stack — an API layer silently dropping a field, a patch-release import break, a monitoring bridge missing the KV-cache metric, and the engine rewinding a request under your own state — none of which the engine benchmark tests.
05·Daleksagordic.com/blog/vllm

Inside vLLM: Anatomy of a High-Throughput LLM Inference System

Aleksa Gordić (Aug 2025). An inverse-pyramid deep dive into vLLM’s V1 engine: the scheduler, PagedAttention, continuous batching, chunked prefill, prefix caching, guided and speculative decoding, disaggregated prefill/decode, multi-GPU/multi-node scaling, the serving layer, and benchmarking with the roofline model. Ties stages 4 and 5 together.
Start at 1. Most people skip to 4 and wonder why nothing clicks.

About this list

A sequential reading path for learning LLM inference, kept in the original post’s five-stage order. Work top to bottom: the foundations and hardware stages (1–3) set up the vocabulary and the memory-bandwidth intuition that the optimization and engine stages (4–5) depend on. Each stage’s chips list the sub-topics it covers.

← Back to home
entry.summary: A curated, sequential reading path for learning LLM inference — foundations, transformers, GPU hardware, optimization techniques, and inference engines.

entry.title: Welcome to my blog
entry.content:
Welcome 👋 This is the first post on my new site.

I plan to use this space as a lab notebook — short technical notes, longer write-ups when I dig into something, and the occasional project retrospective. Topics will mostly orbit machine learning and embedded systems, plus whatever else I happen to be building.

Adding a new post

Posts live in the _posts/ folder as Markdown files named YYYY-MM-DD-title.md. The bit at the top between the --- lines is the front matter — it sets the title, date, description, and tags:

---
layout: post
title: My next post
date: 2026-08-01 10:00:00+0530
description: a one-line summary
tags: machine-learning code
---

Everything below the front matter is just Markdown. Commit the file, push to GitHub, and the site rebuilds and deploys itself automatically.

The next post shows off the formatting features available — code, math, tables, and more. Thanks for stopping by!

entry.title: How to write a post (a living template)

link.title: How to write a post (a living template)

entry.content:
Everything on this page is written in plain Markdown — no HTML, no “code.” The only special part of a post is the little block at the very top (between the --- lines), called the front matter. Notice the sidebar on the left: it’s built automatically from the headings below, and the current section highlights (darkens) as you scroll. That comes from these three lines in the front matter:

toc:
  sidebar: left

Change left to right to move it, or delete those lines to turn it off. To start a new post, just copy this file, rename it, and replace the content.

The front matter

The block at the top sets the post’s metadata. The important fields:

---
layout: post
title: My post title
date: 2026-08-01 09:00:00+0530   # controls ordering; future dates stay hidden until then
description: a one-line summary shown in the blog list
tags: machine-learning embedded   # space-separated
toc:
  sidebar: left
---

Everything below the closing --- is just the post body in Markdown.

Text formatting

You can write bold, italic, inline code, and links.

Blockquotes are great for highlighting a key idea or quoting a source.

  • Bulleted lists
  • work as you’d expect
    • and they nest 1. Numbered lists 2. do too

Code

Fenced code blocks get syntax highlighting for whatever language you tag them with (the ```python on the opening fence):

def fib(n):
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a

Math with LaTeX

Math is written in LaTeX and rendered by MathJax. Surround an expression with $$.

Inline and display

Inside a sentence it stays inline — like $$E = mc^2$$ gives \(E = mc^2\). Put it on its own line and it becomes a centered display equation:

\[\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}}\left[ \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(f_\theta(x), y) \right]\]

Numbered equations

Use an equation environment with a \label{} to get an automatically numbered equation you can reference later with \eqref{}:

\begin{equation} \label{eq:attention} \mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V \end{equation}

We can then point back to equation \eqref{eq:attention} from anywhere in the text.

Tables

Model Params Accuracy
Baseline 1.2M 91.3%
Ours 0.8M 93.7%

Publishing

Save the file in _posts/ named YYYY-MM-DD-title.md, commit it, and push to main. The site rebuilds and redeploys itself in a minute or two — nothing else to do.
entry.summary: Markdown, LaTeX, code, and the scrolling sidebar — copy this file to start a new post.
